q: What is a storage engine?
options: The layer that stores rows on disk and gets them back, beneath parsing and planning
The process that accepts client connections and routes them
The part of the planner that picks an index
The component that ships changes to replicas
why: MySQL lets you choose one per table, which is why the same SQL can behave differently.

q: BEGIN, INSERT, ROLLBACK on a MyISAM table all return OK. Where's the row?
options: Still in the table: MyISAM has no transactions, so ROLLBACK did nothing
Gone: ROLLBACK removed it as usual
In a pending state until the next CHECK TABLE
Visible only to the session that inserted it
why: No error, no warning, and the row was visible to other sessions at once.

q: Why did an update of row 2 wait while another session read row 1 of a MyISAM table?
options: MyISAM locks whole tables, so any read holds up any write
The two rows happened to share a page
MyISAM waits for all reads to commit before any write
An index lock covered both rows
why: On InnoDB, row locks let the same two statements proceed side by side.

q: You create an InnoDB table with no primary key. What does InnoDB do?
options: Adds a hidden clustered index, GEN_CLUST_INDEX
Stores the rows in a heap, as Postgres does
Refuses the CREATE TABLE statement
Uses the first column as the primary key
why: InnoDB always stores a table in a clustered tree, so it makes one up.

q: Is it true that Postgres can't change its table storage?
options: No: table access methods exist since version 12, though only heap ships with it
Yes: heap is built in, and there's no interface for another
Yes, but indexes can be swapped between B-tree and heap
No: you pick an engine per table, as in MySQL
why: The lecture was out of date on that. pg_am lists heap as the one table method.

q: Connection B can't write to a SQLite file while A has a write transaction open, even for another row. What does WAL mode change?
options: Readers and the writer stop blocking each other, and there's still one writer
Several writers can work at once on different tables
Each row gets its own lock, so B's write goes through
B's write queues in the WAL and applies after A commits
why: SQLite's docs are explicit: only one WAL file, so only one writer at a time.

q: What are the only two things a write does in an LSM tree before returning?
options: A log append and a memtable insert
A B-tree insert and a page split
A compaction and a level flush
A file sort and an fsync of every SSTable
why: No page is rewritten in place, which is why real LevelDB took 232,800 writes a second.

q: All 200,000 keys were deleted from LevelDB, and disk use went from 2.9 MB to 4.3 MB. Why?
options: A delete is a new entry, a tombstone, and space only returns at compaction
LevelDB copies deleted keys to a recycle file
The log file grew because deletes can't be batched
Deletes rewrite each SSTable with a larger page size
why: compactRange then took it to zero, which also disproves the lecture's 'nothing is ever deleted'.

q: Why might a read in an LSM tree check several files?
options: The newest version of a key could be in any level, so it's checked newest first
Each key is split across several files
Reads have to wait for compaction to finish first
Every file holds a part of the row
why: That's why engines keep a Bloom filter per file, and it's the cost of fast writes.

q: A crash wipes an LSM tree's memtable. What brings it back?
options: Replaying the write-ahead log
Reading the highest level's newest file
A background compaction
Nothing: unflushed writes are lost by design
why: Like any engine, an LSM tree logs before it acknowledges a write.

q: A cursor returned 50 rows in about 1 ms, where a plain SELECT took 1.5 seconds. Did it do less total work?
options: No: it spreads the work out, as FETCH LAST taking longer shows
Yes: a cursor skips rows the client doesn't read
Yes: cursors read an index rather than the table
No, and it's slower overall, since it runs the query twice
why: The win is the first row and client memory, 365 MB in that run.

q: A client pages through a server-side cursor for minutes. What does that hold open?
options: A transaction, which holds locks and blocks DDL, and keeps old row versions alive
Only a small amount of client memory
A second copy of the table on the server
An exclusive lock on every row read
why: The replay showed ALTER TABLE waiting until the cursor's transaction ended.

q: Which is a fair correction of the talk's engine history?
options: XtraDB is Percona's fork of InnoDB, and Sleepycat made Berkeley DB
XtraDB is MySQL AB's original engine, and Sleepycat made SQLite
MongoDB switched to RocksDB as its default in 2020
LevelDB has no form of atomic write at all
why: MySQL AB was the Swedish company. LevelDB's README lists atomic batches. MongoRocks was never MongoDB's default.

q: Why does a normal MongoDB find by _id take two tree walks?
options: The _id index gives a recordId, and a hidden tree maps that to the document
Every lookup checks both the primary and a replica
BSON documents are split across two trees
WiredTiger reads the index twice to verify it
why: That keeps index values small, at the cost of a second walk.

q: What changes in a clustered collection?
options: Documents live in the _id tree, so there's one walk and no separate _id index
Documents are spread across several servers
Documents are stored in a column layout
The collection is held entirely in memory
why: The real stats showed no _id_ index at all. It's InnoDB's design, including the cost of a long key.

q: What page sizes did the collection's WiredTiger settings actually show?
options: Internal pages 4 KB, and leaf pages up to 32 KB
All pages 4 KB, as the lecture said
All pages 8 KB, the same as Postgres
All pages 16 KB, the same as InnoDB
why: Read from the collection's creationString. The lecture's 4 KB was only half right.

q: A Mongo plan has FETCH over IXSCAN. What's the SQL equivalent?
options: An index scan followed by reading the row from the table
A sequential scan with a filter
An index-only scan
A bitmap AND of two indexes
why: With a projection covering the query, totalDocsExamined fell to 0, the same idea as index-only.

q: Why does Memcached use slab classes?
options: Fixed-size chunks avoid the fragmentation of allocating items of every size
They let items be compressed by size
They keep related keys next to each other
They allow different eviction rules for each client
why: The price is waste: an item takes a whole chunk, and a 100-byte value took 192 bytes.

q: Which happens when you exceed a Memcached limit?
options: A 2 MB value gets SERVER_ERROR object too large, and a 251-character key gets a client error
Large values are split across several chunks automatically
Long keys are hashed down to fit
The server grows its memory past -m to fit the item
why: Limits of 250 characters and 1 MB by default, both confirmed on a real server.

q: Memcached server 2 of 3 dies. What happens to the others?
options: Nothing: servers never talk, so only server 2's keys become misses
They rebalance its keys between them
They stop serving until a new server joins
One of them takes over its hash range and copies its data
why: The client's hash picks the server. In the run: 2,000 hits, 1,000 lost.

q: Redis went from about 69,000 to over a million requests a second with -P 16. What changed?
options: Pipelining: commands are sent without waiting for each reply, removing round trips
It switched from one thread to sixteen
It turned off persistence during the test
It batched the keys into one larger key
why: Same single thread. Most of the time had been going on the network.

q: What's a risk of Redis running commands on one thread?
options: One slow command, such as KEYS * on a big database, stalls everyone
Two commands can interleave and corrupt a value
Pub/sub messages can arrive out of order
Keys can't expire while a command is running
why: The same design makes each command atomic with no locks.

q: A Redis server was killed mid-write under each setting. What did the run show?
options: No persistence lost everything, RDB lost 235 keys, and AOF lost none
All settings lost about the same number of keys
RDB lost nothing, and AOF lost up to a second
Every setting lost everything, because data lives in memory
why: AOF with fsync on every write ran about 9 times slower, the true price of fsync.

q: Why did AOF with everysec lose nothing in the kill test, though the docs say it can lose a second?
options: Writes had reached the OS, which survives a process kill: a power cut could still lose them
Redis flushed the buffer on receiving the kill signal
The test ran for less than a second
Docker snapshots the file system at the moment of the kill
why: The same caveat as the Postgres crash test.

q: A Redis subscriber joins after a message was published. What does it receive?
options: Nothing: pub/sub is fire and forget, and messages aren't stored
The last message on that channel
Every message from the last hour
An error saying that it missed messages
why: Use streams if messages must wait for a consumer.

q: Postgres won't start with ssl=on and a key file that's readable by everyone. Why?
options: It refuses a private key with group or world access: chmod 600 restricts it
It needs chmod 600 so that the key can be executed
Keys must be owned by root to be loaded
The certificate and key must have the same permissions
why: The lecture said chmod 600 allows execution. It restricts reading to the owner.

q: TLS is on, yet a client connects without it. What stops that?
options: A hostssl line in pg_hba.conf, which only matches TLS connections
Setting ssl = required in postgresql.conf
Removing the password from the role
Nothing on the server: only the client can decide
why: ssl=on only makes TLS available. pg_hba.conf decides who must use it.

q: What does a client see when it verifies a self-signed certificate?
options: A failure, because no trusted authority signed it
A successful connection, but with no encryption
A warning in the server's log only
Nothing: certificates aren't checked for databases
why: Encryption without verification protects against eavesdropping, and not an impostor.

q: On an unencrypted Postgres connection, what could someone on the path read?
options: The query text and the results, though not the password itself under SCRAM
Only the table names
Nothing, since the wire protocol is binary
The password, but not the queries
why: The capture found the query's text in plain sight. With TLS, the same search found nothing.

q: What's the default password scheme in current Postgres?
options: scram-sha-256, where the password never crosses the wire
md5, as in the lecture's capture
Plain text inside a TLS tunnel
SHA-1 with a per-user salt
why: It became the default in version 14. The lecture's capture was of an older server.

q: An insert-only role gets 'permission denied for sequence todos_id_seq'. Why?
options: A serial column needs USAGE on its sequence as well as INSERT on the table
Inserts need SELECT on the table first
The sequence belongs to another schema
Roles can't use sequences without superuser rights
why: Exactly the failure the course hit. The fix is GRANT USAGE ON SEQUENCE.

q: A role with only DELETE runs DELETE FROM todos WHERE id = 1 and is denied. Why?
options: Reading the WHERE column needs SELECT
DELETE always needs TRUNCATE as well
The role needs USAGE on the primary key index
A DELETE with a WHERE clause needs table ownership
why: So 'least privilege' is less obvious than it looks. You have to test each role.

q: How does a read-only role limit a SQL injection?
options: An injected DROP or DELETE fails, because the role doesn't have the right
It stops the injected SQL from being parsed
It encrypts the query before it's sent
It removes UNION from the allowed syntax
why: Parameters stop injection. Roles limit the blast radius if one gets through.

q: Why should an app's user not run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at startup?
options: Its role shouldn't own the schema, and since version 15 it can't create in public by default
It's too slow to run on every start
IF NOT EXISTS can silently drop data
It holds an exclusive lock for the app's whole lifetime
why: Schema changes belong to a separate owner role. The course's answer to the question.

q: What's the better way to send a million ids to a query?
options: One array parameter with = ANY($1), not a huge OR built as text
A million separate queries over one connection
A temporary view holding the text of the query
Raising the server's maximum query length
why: The text version has to be sent, parsed and planned. It's also how the course crashed a free database.

q: What does homomorphic encryption let a server do?
options: Compute on data it can't read
Decrypt data without the key, using a proof
Encrypt data faster than AES
Store data without using any key
why: The browser demo adds salaries by multiplying ciphertexts, and only the client can decrypt the total.

q: The lecture says nobody encrypts data in a database. What's the fair correction?
options: Data at rest is often encrypted, and the gap is data in use, while it's being computed on
All databases encrypt every column by default
Encryption is impossible for indexed columns
TLS covers data at rest too
why: Three states: in transit, at rest, in use. Homomorphic encryption targets the third.

q: What happens when a client connects to Postgres?
options: The postmaster forks a new backend process for it
A thread from a shared pool picks it up
It joins a single event loop in the main process
A replica takes it if the primary is busy
why: That's why pools matter, and why settings such as work_mem multiply with connections.

q: The same UPDATE wrote 5,758 kB of WAL after a checkpoint, then 231 kB. Why the gap?
options: The first change to a page after a checkpoint logs the whole page
The first run also had to build the index
WAL compression only starts after a few writes
The second run wrote its changes to an undo log instead
why: full_page_writes protect against torn pages. More frequent checkpoints mean more of this.

q: Why does Postgres have no undo log?
options: Old row versions stay in the table, so rollback only has to mark a transaction aborted
It keeps undo records in the WAL instead
It doesn't support rollback for large transactions
Each transaction works on a private copy of the page
why: Rollback is instant, and VACUUM is the bill.

q: Recovery replays changes from a transaction that never committed. Why doesn't that show wrong data?
options: With no commit record, those row versions stay invisible
Recovery skips any record that has no commit record
They're undone by reading the undo log afterwards
A checkpoint deletes uncommitted pages first
why: Replay only rebuilds pages. Visibility decides what anyone can see.

q: Three UPDATEs took a table from 3.5 MB to 14 MB. VACUUM ran, and it stayed at 14 MB. Why?
options: VACUUM makes space reusable, and only VACUUM FULL returns it to the operating system
VACUUM only removes rows older than a day
The space is held for the WAL until the next checkpoint
Autovacuum has to run first, and then VACUUM has an effect
why: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under an exclusive lock, which brought it back to 3.5 MB.

q: VACUUM reports nothing removed, and 1,000 dead rows remain. What's the likely reason?
options: An open transaction has a snapshot that could still need those versions
The table is too small for vacuum to run
Autovacuum is holding a lock on it
Dead rows are only removed once a day
why: One long transaction holds back cleanup for the whole server.

q: What must be true for a HOT update?
options: No indexed column changes, and the new version fits on the same page
The table has no indexes at all
The update changes only the primary key
The transaction runs at SERIALIZABLE
why: Then the index keeps pointing at the old line pointer, and the chain continues inside the page.

q: Updating an indexed column wrote more WAL with each extra index, even on other columns. Why?
options: The new version has a new address, so every index needs a new entry
Every index is rebuilt on each update
The WAL records all index contents at each commit
Indexes are compressed on every write
why: From 15 MB to 59 MB with five indexes. That's write amplification, and the heart of Uber's complaint.

q: Why does the same update touch fewer structures in InnoDB?
options: Secondary indexes hold the primary key, which didn't change, so they're left alone
InnoDB doesn't keep secondary indexes up to date until a read
InnoDB compresses index updates into one write
InnoDB has no write-ahead log to update
why: It pays for that on reads, with a second tree walk.

q: A bulk update of an unindexed column was only 4,368 of 10,000 HOT. Why not all?
options: The free space on each page ran out, so the rest of the rows had to move
HOT is limited to a fixed number of rows per statement
The other updates changed an indexed column
Autovacuum interrupted the statement
why: fillfactor reserves room for HOT, and a bulk update quickly uses it up.

q: SELECT id FROM t WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT parent FROM t) returns nothing. The subquery contains a NULL. Why?
options: Comparing with NULL gives unknown, so no row can pass the test
NOT IN removes NULL rows, and then fails on an empty list
NULL is treated as 0, which matches every id
Subqueries with NULLs are rejected, and return no rows
why: Filter the nulls out, or use NOT EXISTS.

q: SELECT * took 297 ms and SELECT id took 5 ms on the same rows. What's a cause that an index can't fix?
options: Large out-of-line values had to be read and sent to the client
SELECT * always runs without a query plan
The star has to be expanded at runtime for each row
SELECT * takes a table lock for the whole scan
why: It also lost the index-only scan: 753 pages against 17, and 47 MB delivered.

q: A prepared transaction survived SIGKILL. What's the catch?
options: It keeps its locks until someone decides, so an orphan blocks work and vacuum
It's rolled back at the next checkpoint
It can only be committed from the original connection
It loses its changes, and only its id survives
why: The docs warn that it's meant for a real transaction manager and not for applications.
